rows.answer:
That's not really how I work — I don't run decisions through a named framework.

What I actually do is closer to: slow down before touching anything, figure out what's really happening versus what someone thinks is happening, then work out what the constraint actually is before proposing a solution.

On the current consulting project, the first move was deliberately not to open a single tool. I ran a structured discovery process — interview scripts, templates, transcripts — specifically to separate what the owner believed was true from what the data would later show. That gap turned out to be significant. The stacked discount problem, for example, wasn't visible to anyone until we had a clean dataset to look at it properly.

The other thing I pay attention to is whether a problem is actually a system problem or a training and process problem dressed up as one. A lot of what looks like a technology gap on the floor is really an adoption gap. That shapes what I recommend — and it usually means the answer is cheaper and faster than buying something new.

If there's a principle underneath all of it, it's probably: the best solution is the one the client can actually sustain without you. Analytical findings nobody can execute are worthless.
